checkpoints: Building a physical filename by concatenating a timestamp with `file.originalname` embeds client-controlled input directly into a filesystem path — a value like `../../../etc/cron.d/evil` walks the write straight out of the intended upload directory, which is a path-traversal vulnerability, not a cosmetic naming issue.

The safe fix for path traversal is not just stripping `../` — it is to stop using client input in the physical path at all: reduce it to `path.basename()` at minimum, or better, generate the on-disk filename from a server-side UUID and keep the client's original filename only as DB metadata for display and download.

`file.mimetype` in Multer is populated verbatim from the `Content-Type` header of the multipart part, a value the client sets and fully controls — it is not derived from inspecting the file's actual bytes, so an allow-list check against it can be trivially bypassed by relabeling any file with an allowed Content-Type.

An extension- or declared-type allow-list is a reasonable first filter but is not sufficient on its own for production; it needs a magic-byte / content-sniffing layer (e.g. reading the leading bytes with a library like `file-type`) added on top of it, since a renamed executable sent with a spoofed `image/jpeg` header will otherwise pass untouched.

Using `Date.now()` alone as the uniqueness component of a generated filename only guarantees millisecond resolution — two requests arriving in the same millisecond, or two application instances behind a load balancer generating filenames independently, can produce an identical filename and silently overwrite one upload with another with no error raised.

When `diskStorage` writes the uploaded file to disk before any application-level validation (such as checking image dimensions) runs, a rejection at that later validation step leaves the already-written file orphaned on disk; the rejection path must explicitly delete the file (e.g. `fs.promises.unlink(file.path)`) or storage will slowly fill with rejected uploads over time.

In a code review, security-relevant defects like path traversal and spoofable content-type trust are blockers that should gate approval outright, while correctness and hygiene issues like filename collisions and orphaned files are must-fix-before-merge items — distinguishing the two categories, and pairing each finding with a concrete required fix rather than a vague call to "harden this," is itself part of reviewing well.

Verifying these fixes requires concrete evidence rather than trusting the fix on faith: a test uploading a filename containing traversal segments that must not land outside the upload directory, a test with a mislabeled binary payload that must be rejected, a concurrency test proving two same-instant uploads don't collide, and a test asserting no file remains on disk after a failed validation step.
